connections.observation: σωφροσύνη/ἐγκράτεια (s001) names the virtue the young must acquire; καρτερίαι and the Odyssean τέτλαθι/ἔτλης (s010) supply its approved exemplars. The contrast between Zeus ἐπιλανθανόμενον/ἐκπλαγέντα and Odysseus addressing his heart makes visible that self-mastery requires precisely the endurance that Zeus, in his desire, lacks.

The concrete cluster of πότους, ἀφροδίσια, ἐδωδάς (s004) names what the young must rule as ἄρχοντας ἡδονῶν (s006); Zeus's ἐπιθυμία τῶν ἀφροδισίων then enacts the failure of such rule. The section's opening prescription becomes visibly violated in the divine exemplar it cites.

πείθω moves through three zones: Homeric command (ἐπιπείθεο), gifts persuading gods (πείθει), and repeated verbal forms governing what the νέοι should πείθεσθαι or not (s003). The young (s007) are positioned throughout as those who must be protected from persuasion by harmful poetry, making persuasion itself the contested instrument of their formation.

δῶρα recur densely (s002) in connection with Achilles and the definition of the men as δωροδόκους and φιλοχρημάτους; ἄρχοντας (s005) appears as both the internal rulers of pleasures and the external rulers whom private citizens insolently address. Gifts corrupt both relations of rule: they replace obedience to ἄρχοντας and show the failure to be ἄρχοντας over one's own desires.

Divine parentage (s009)—θεᾶς παῖς, θεοῦ παῖδα, θεῶν ἀγχίσποροι, αἷμα δαιμόνων—makes Achilles' νοσήματε δύο ἐναντίω (s014) more perceptible as a scandal: one born of a goddess and Peleus σωφρονεστάτου, educated by Chiron σοφώτατος, yet containing opposite diseases. The genealogical concentration makes the distance between divine origin and actual conduct newly visible.

The verbal adjectives in -τέον (s008)—θεατέον, ἀκουστέον, ἐατέον, πειστέον, παυστέον, λεκτέον—prescribe what must be done regarding poetic content; ἀκούω recurs (s016) as the specific activity the young perform. Held together, they make visible that hearing (ἀκούειν) is the site requiring legislative control through prescriptive forms, culminating in the judgment that certain content is βλαβερά to ἀκούουσιν.

The descending sequence θεῶν, δαιμόνων, ἡρώων, τῶν ἐν Ἅιδου, ἀνθρώπων (s011) reaches its final term as the one that is ἀδύνατον to settle now (s012). The completed topics frame humans as λοιπόν; the impossibility of settling what to say about them makes visible that the entire legislative sequence arrests at the threshold of its own subject.

The impossibility (ἀδύνατον) of settling what to say about humans (s012) is grounded in the poets' paired contrasts (s013): ἄδικοι εὐδαίμονες versus δίκαιοι ἄθλιοι, justice as ἀλλότριον ἀγαθόν versus οἰκεία ζημία. These contrasts cannot be legislated against until δικαιοσύνη is found; the section makes visible that its own prescriptive project depends on a discovery not yet made.

σωφροσύνη opens the section as what is needed (s001), with Peleus named σωφρονεστάτου (s001); Achilles is then said to contain νοσήματε δύο ἐναντίω ἀλλήλοιν (s014), including ἀνελευθερίαν μετὰ φιλοχρηματίας. The superlative σωφροσύνη attributed to the father makes the son's opposite diseases a reversal, visible as a failed transmission from σωφρονεστάτου to one full of ταραχή.

δῶρα θεοὺς πείθει (s002, s003) states the quoted maxim; δῶρα then recurs three more times regarding Achilles, while πείθω multiplies through πείθεσθαι, πειστέον, πείθειν, πεισθείς. The conjunction makes visible that gifts and persuasion are coupled instruments: gifts persuade gods and rulers, while the young must be prevented from being persuaded by poetry that teaches this coupling.

The concrete pleasures of πότους, ἀφροδίσια, ἐδωδάς, and the feast scene (s004) are set against καρτερίαι and the Odyssean τέτλαθι δή, κραδίη (s010). Zeus ἐπιλανθανόμενον through ἀφροδισίων ἐπιθυμίαν enacts the failure to endure, making visible the opposition between endurance addressing one's own heart and desire overcoming divine deliberation.

The young (s007) must be ὑπηκόους to ἄρχοντας and ἄρχοντας of pleasures (s005); yet they are also exposed to νεανιεύματα ἰδιωτῶν εἰς ἄρχοντας (s005). The lexical echo between νεανίαις and νεανιεύματα makes visible that the young are both the subject requiring formation and the word for insolent speech against rulers, linking their identity to the very behaviour they must avoid.

ἡδονή (s006) first appears as what the young must rule, then as ἄλλην ἡδονήν such poetry might provide; the poets claim (s013) that δικαιοσύνη is ἀλλότριον ἀγαθόν, οἰκεία ζημία. Held together, ἄλλην and ἀλλότριον/οἰκεία make visible an opposition between own and other's: pleasure may be another's, justice may belong to another rather than oneself, configuring a recurrent question of possession and benefit.

elements.context: οὐ γὰρ οἶμαι εἴς γε σωφροσύνην νέοις ἐπιτήδεια ἀκούειν
δοκεῖ σοι ἐπιτήδειον εἶναι πρὸς ἐγκράτειαν ἑαυτοῦ ἀκούειν νέῳ

new_signals.observation: ἐπιτήδειος recurs twice in rapid succession, both times qualifying what is suitable for the young to hear in relation to σωφροσύνη and ἐγκράτεια.

elements.context: τὰ δὴ τοιάδε φήσομεν οἶμαι καλῶς λέγεσθαι
καὶ τὰ τούτων ἑξῆς ἆρα καλῶς

new_signals.observation: καλῶς appears three times affirming Homeric examples, then negated (οὐ καλῶς) for insolent speech, creating a local pattern of judgment.

elements.context: λέγοντα ὡς οὕτως ὑπὸ ἐπιθυμίας ἔχεται
περὶ γὰρ θεῶν ὡς δεῖ λέγεσθαι εἴρηται

new_signals.observation: λέγω appears in varied forms throughout: infinitives regarding what should be said, participles of those speaking, finite verbs of actual speech, and the verbal adjective λεκτέον prescribing what must be said.

elements.context: σωφροσύνης δὲ ὡς πλήθει οὐ τὰ τοιάδε μέγιστα
τὰ δὴ τοιάδε φήσομεν οἶμαι καλῶς λέγεσθαι

new_signals.observation: τὰ τοιάδε recurs three times in close succession, each time introducing a category of poetic content for judgment.

elements.context: Πηλέως, σωφρονεστάτου τε καὶ τρίτου ἀπὸ Διός

new_signals.observation: Peleus is positioned as third from Zeus, making Achilles fourth; the numbered genealogical distance from the divine is marked precisely.
βλάπτω appears first in Achilles' quoted accusation against Apollo (ἔβλαψάς), then returns as the judgment that such stories are βλαβερά to listeners.
